title: Overview of research progress and application of experimental models of colorectal cancer

subsections.section_title: In Vitro Cellular Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.content:
Organoid models have become one of the most informative in vitro platforms for colorectal cancer (CRC) because they preserve three-dimensional architecture, multilineage differentiation, and key patient-specific genomic features more faithfully than conventional monolayer cultures. Conceptually, organoids are self-organizing structures derived from pluripotent or adult stem/progenitor cells that recapitulate essential aspects of organ development and tissue function, making them particularly suitable for modeling intestinal homeostasis and neoplastic transformation ref [1], ref [2].

In CRC research, long-term organoid culture from normal intestine and colon established the technical basis for patient-derived tumor organoids, while human intestinal differentiation from pluripotent stem cells clarified developmental routes relevant to epithelial specification ref [3], ref [4], ref [5]. Subsequent studies showed that adenoma and adenocarcinoma organoids can be propagated from patient material and retain major histologic and mutational features, enabling living biobanks that capture interpatient heterogeneity ref [6], ref [7]. Genome engineering further strengthened causality by reconstructing stepwise colorectal tumorigenesis through APC, KRAS, TP53, and SMAD4 pathway alterations in human intestinal organoids ref [8].

Functionally, CRC organoids are valuable for drug screening, biomarker discovery, and precision oncology because ex vivo treatment responses can reflect clinically relevant subtype-specific vulnerabilities ref [7], ref [9]. They also support studies of cancer stemness, invasion, metastatic fitness, and host-pathogen interactions, especially when combined with orthotopic transplantation, air-liquid interface systems, immune co-culture, or fibroblast-containing platforms ref [10], ref [11], ref [12], ref [13]. However, limitations remain, including variable extracellular matrices, selective growth conditions, incomplete stromal and vascular representation, and evolutionary drift during prolonged culture ref [1], ref [2], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: In Vitro Cellular Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Broader Conceptual and Translational Context for In Vitro Tumor Models
subsections.content:
In vitro tumor models should be viewed within a broader conceptual framework in which experimental utility is judged by how well a system captures core cancer phenotypes while remaining tractable for mechanistic study. The updated hallmarks of cancer emphasize that malignant behavior emerges not only from proliferative signaling and resistance to cell death, but also from deregulated metabolism, immune evasion, phenotypic plasticity, nonmutational reprogramming, and reciprocal interactions with stromal and inflammatory compartments ref [2]. For colorectal cancer (CRC), this implies that model selection is not merely a technical issue, but a biological decision about which layers of tumor complexity are most relevant to the question being asked.

From a translational standpoint, conventional 2D monolayers remain indispensable for standardized, low-cost, and high-throughput interrogation of gene function and drug sensitivity, yet they incompletely represent tissue polarity, extracellular matrix constraints, oxygen and nutrient gradients, and multicellular crosstalk. These shortcomings are particularly consequential for therapies whose activity depends on microenvironmental context, including immunotherapy ref [3]. Three-dimensional systems partially bridge this gap by better recapitulating diffusion barriers, spatial heterogeneity, and cell-state diversity, thereby improving evaluation of antibody penetration, immune-cell infiltration, and adaptive resistance programs ref [3].

Accordingly, in vitro CRC modeling is increasingly organized as a continuum rather than a hierarchy: simple cell lines support reductionist discovery, spheroids and colospheres model architecture and stress gradients, and organoid or chip-based platforms extend toward patient-specific prediction. No single platform fully reproduces vasculature, microbiota, systemic immunity, or metastatic niche effects, so translational confidence usually depends on convergent evidence across complementary systems. In this sense, the value of in vitro models lies less in replacing in vivo studies than in enabling iterative, human-relevant hypothesis testing, biomarker discovery, and rational preclinical prioritization for precision oncology ref [3], ref [2].

subsections.section_title: In Vitro Cellular Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations and Limitations of In Vitro CRC Cell Culture
subsections.content:
In vitro cell culture underpins modern colorectal cancer (CRC) research, but its conceptual foundations predate oncology-specific models. Early tissue culture work established that isolated cells could survive and proliferate outside the organism, while also revealing that growth depends critically on microenvironmental conditions rather than simple transfer to an artificial vessel ref [5], ref [6]. This historical trajectory supports the use of CRC cultures as reductionist systems for interrogating proliferation, signaling, metabolism, and drug response, with the practical advantages of experimental control, scalability, and accessibility over animal or clinical studies ref [4], ref [6].

At the same time, the earliest cell-culture literature already foreshadowed major limitations that remain relevant to CRC models. Sanford, Earle, and Likely showed that single-cell growth required restricted culture volume and conditioned medium, emphasizing that survival and clonogenic expansion are shaped by paracrine support and media composition ref [5]. More broadly, long-term culture selects for variants adapted to artificial conditions, and immortalized lines can undergo phenotypic drift, clonal selection, and divergence from the source tumor over serial passage ref [6], ref [4], ref [5]. These issues are especially important in CRC, where intratumoral heterogeneity, stromal signaling, hypoxia, and microbiota-related influences are central to disease biology yet are poorly represented in conventional monolayer systems ref [4], ref [6], ref [7].

Accordingly, in vitro CRC culture is best viewed as a foundational but incomplete platform. Conventional culture remains indispensable for mechanistic dissection and high-throughput perturbation, but its findings require careful validation in higher-complexity systems and, ultimately, in vivo or clinical settings ref [4], ref [6]. Attention to authentication, passage history, medium formulation, and culture geometry is therefore essential if these models are to generate reproducible and translationally meaningful insights in CRC research ref [6], ref [5], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: In Vitro Cellular Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.content:
Three-dimensional spheroid systems occupy an intermediate position between conventional monolayer culture and in vivo tumors, reproducing key features of avascular colorectal cancer growth that are largely absent in two-dimensional models. Compared with flat cultures, spheroids generate gradients of oxygen, nutrients, pH, and catabolites, thereby producing proliferative outer layers and quiescent or necrotic inner regions that better approximate solid-tumor architecture and treatment response ref [7], ref [4]. These properties have made multicellular spheroids a standard platform for studying CRC growth kinetics, cell death, radiation response, and limited drug penetration ref [7], ref [4].

In CRC research, spheroids are typically generated from established cell lines under non-adherent conditions, including liquid-overlay, spinner, or rotation-based methods, and can display extracellular-matrix deposition, altered adhesion-molecule expression, and integrin profiles closer to xenografts than to monolayers ref [7], ref [4], ref [5]. Importantly, 3D growth often increases resistance to chemotherapy and irradiation relative to 2D culture, reflecting multicellular resistance mechanisms and microenvironment-dependent phenotypes rather than simple clonal differences ref [7], ref [6], ref [7]. These features have supported the use of CRC spheroids in preclinical drug testing and in studies of invasion-associated signaling and epithelial plasticity ref [4], ref [8], ref [9].

A notable CRC-specific extension of the spheroid concept is the ex vivo colosphere model, generated directly from mechanically dissociated primary colon tumors. Unlike conventional spheroids assembled from long-term cell lines, colospheres form rapidly from patient-derived cancer cells, are absent in paired normal mucosa, and were reported to correlate with advanced AJCC stage and metastatic potential ref [8]. Relative to matched spheroids, colospheres showed weaker junctional organization, detectable MMP-2/MMP-9 activity, greater single-cell escape into Matrigel, and superior tumorigenic and metastatic behavior in vivo, suggesting particular utility for modeling aggressive CRC phenotypes ref [8]. Nevertheless, both spheroids and colospheres remain reductionist systems that incompletely capture stromal, immune, and vascular components, so they are best viewed as complementary 3D platforms bridging simple cell-line assays and more complex organoid or in vivo models ref [8], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: In Vitro Cellular Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Conventional Colorectal Cancer Cell Lines as Experimental Models
subsections.content:
Conventional colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines remain the most widely used in vitro models because they are inexpensive, experimentally tractable, and suitable for mechanistic studies, genetic perturbation, and medium-throughput drug screening. Their principal strength is the availability of well-established lines spanning major CRC molecular subtypes, allowing hypothesis-driven model selection rather than treating cell lines as interchangeable surrogates of disease ref [10].

A key advance has been the systematic molecular annotation and authentication of these models. In a panel of 24 colon cancer cell lines, Ahmed et al. confirmed identities by short tandem repeat profiling and showed substantial diversity in microsatellite instability, CpG island methylator phenotype, and driver alterations in KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, PTEN, and TP53 ref [10]. Such datasets are particularly valuable because misidentification, patient-duplicate lines such as DLD-1/HCT-15 and HT-29/WiDr, and culture adaptation can otherwise confound interpretation ref [10]. Thus, rigorous authentication and genotype-aware selection are prerequisites for reproducible CRC cell-line research.

Functionally, conventional cell lines have also been central to pharmacologic discovery. In 11 colon-cancer cell lines, sensitivity to aspirin, sulindac, sulindac sulfide, and sulindac sulfone was markedly heterogeneous, with SW480 and SW948 showing high sensitivity and WiDr or SNU-C4 relative resistance ref [11]. Sulindac additionally induced cell-cycle perturbation, morphological changes, and broad transcriptional responses in HT-29 cells, illustrating how monolayer cultures can reveal drug-response programs and candidate therapeutic targets ref [11].

Nevertheless, these models incompletely capture tumor architecture, stromal and immune interactions, and intratumoral heterogeneity, and prolonged passage may further select clones that diverge from primary tumors ref [10]. Accordingly, conventional CRC cell lines are best viewed as reductionist but indispensable platforms: ideal for controlled mechanistic and comparative studies, yet most informative when integrated with three-dimensional systems, organoids, and in vivo validation.

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Experimental Animal Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.content:
Chemical carcinogen-induced rodent models remain foundational for studying colorectal tumor initiation because they reproduce stepwise adenoma-to-adenocarcinoma progression within an intact immune, stromal, and metabolic milieu. The most widely used agents are 1,2-dimethylhydrazine (DMH) and its proximate metabolite azoxymethane (AOM), which reliably induce predominantly distal colonic neoplasms in rats and mice and have therefore become standard platforms for intervention and promotion studies ref [2], ref [3], ref [4], ref [5]. Earlier aromatic amine models, especially 3,2′-dimethyl-4-aminobiphenyl (DMAB), were also important in establishing experimental intestinal carcinogenesis, although they produce broader tissue tropism and are now used less often than AOM/DMH ref [12], ref [6], ref [7].

A major strength of these models is their sensitivity to environmental modulation. In F344 rats, dietary wheat bran significantly reduced the incidence and multiplicity of DMAB-induced colon tumors, while citrus fiber was more protective in the small intestine, underscoring that tumor outcome depends on both carcinogen metabolism and fiber type ref [12]. Comparable observations were reported in AOM- or DMH-based systems using wheat bran, pectin, or cellulose, although not all studies agreed, reflecting differences in strain, carcinogen dose, fat content, and timing of dietary intervention ref [3], ref [4], ref [5], ref [8], ref [9], ref [10], ref [11]. This susceptibility to dietary and luminal factors is particularly useful for modeling gene–environment interactions relevant to sporadic colorectal cancer.

Nevertheless, carcinogen models have limitations. Tumor multiplicity and anatomical distribution are highly protocol-dependent, extraintestinal tumors may occur with some agents such as DMAB, and the mutational spectra do not fully mirror genetically engineered or human mismatch-repair-deficient cancers ref [12], ref [6], ref [7], ref [12]. To improve translational relevance, AOM is often combined with dextran sodium sulfate (AOM/DSS) to couple mutagenesis with inflammation-driven promotion, generating rapid colitis-associated colorectal tumors ref [13], ref [14]. Accordingly, chemical carcinogenesis models are best viewed as versatile in vivo systems for studying initiation, promotion, dietary modulation, and chemoprevention rather than as universal surrogates for every molecular subtype of colorectal cancer.

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Experimental Animal Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Dietary and Molecular Risk Factors Relevant to Animal Modeling
subsections.content:
Dietary and host-associated risk factors are highly relevant when designing in vivo colorectal cancer (CRC) models, because they shape not only tumor incidence but also anatomic distribution and molecular phenotype. Epidemiologic data indicate that a Western dietary pattern, enriched in red and processed meat, refined grains, and added sugars, is associated with increased CRC risk, whereas prudent diets rich in fruits, vegetables, fish, and whole grains are associated with lower risk ref [13]. Importantly, the excess risk linked to Western diets appears stronger for distal colon and rectal tumors and tends to associate with MSS, KRAS-wildtype, BRAF-wildtype, and CIMP-low/negative cancers ref [13].

These observations provide a rationale for incorporating diet as an experimental variable in rodent studies rather than treating it as background husbandry. High-fat or meat-associated diets can be used to model promotion of chromosomal-instability-like tumorigenesis, while fiber-rich or otherwise protective diets may be useful for prevention studies and for testing interactions with inflammatory tone, microbial metabolites, and carcinogen exposure. Because proximal and distal bowel segments differ in embryologic origin, luminal metabolites, and microbiota, dietary interventions may also influence tumor location-specific outcomes, which should be recorded systematically in animal experiments ref [13].

Molecular susceptibility is equally important. APC dysregulation is central to the traditional adenoma-carcinoma sequence and remains especially pertinent for models intended to mimic distal, chromosomally unstable CRC. By contrast, mismatch-repair-deficient settings, including hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, can show somatic APC alterations but follow a distinct molecular context ref [14]. Thus, animal model selection should align dietary exposure with the intended genetic background—for example, APC-mutant strains for conventional adenomatous pathways versus MMR-deficient models for MSI-associated disease—so that diet-gene interactions are biologically interpretable and translationally relevant.

subsections.section_title: In Vivo Experimental Animal Models of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Organoid Systems as Adjuncts Rather Than In Vivo Models
subsections.content:
Organoid platforms have become important complements to colorectal cancer animal research because they preserve three-dimensional epithelial architecture, patient-specific genotypes, and aspects of intratumoral heterogeneity that are poorly represented in conventional two-dimensional cultures ref [15]. However, they should not be classified as in vivo models: organoids are generated and maintained ex vivo, generally lack vasculature, immune, stromal, neural, and endocrine system integration, and cannot reproduce whole-organism phenomena such as metastatic dissemination, cachexia, pharmacokinetics, or host inflammatory responses ref [15]. Their value in this survey is therefore best understood as adjunctive rather than substitutive to rodent models.

For colorectal cancer specifically, patient-derived organoids can faithfully retain histopathologic and molecular features of the source tumor and are well suited for parallel functional testing of drug sensitivity and resistance. Living biobank studies showed that colorectal cancer organoids preserve driver alterations and can support genotype–drug correlation analyses, while metastatic gastrointestinal organoid cohorts further demonstrated concordance between ex vivo drug response and patient clinical outcome, including resistance evolution during therapy ref [16]. These properties make organoids especially useful for hypothesis generation, biomarker prioritization, and co-clinical study design before validation in chemically induced, genetically engineered, or xenograft-based in vivo systems ref [16].

At the same time, the current limitations of organoid technology explain why it cannot replace animal models in studies of colorectal carcinogenesis. Reviews of the field emphasize variability in architecture, dependence on extracellular matrices such as Matrigel, and incomplete representation of the tumor microenvironment; even with co-culture refinements, organoids remain reductionist systems relative to intact organisms ref [15]. Thus, in colorectal cancer research, organoids are best deployed alongside rather than against in vivo models: they improve mechanistic resolution and patient relevance, whereas animal models remain indispensable for investigating diet–host interactions, immune surveillance, angiogenesis, metastatic niche formation, and systemic therapeutic toxicity.

subsections.subsection_title: Figure-Based Models of Early Colon Carcinogenesis
subsections.content:
Figure-based depictions of early colon carcinogenesis have historically centered on aberrant crypt foci (ACF), which provide a visually tractable intermediate between normal mucosa and adenomatous change. Classic methylene-blue whole-mount imaging and histologic validation established ACF as quantifiable preneoplastic lesions in carcinogen-treated rodent colon, enabling figure panels that link crypt enlargement, pericryptal elevation, and multiplicity to progressive risk ref [2], ref [3], ref [4], ref [5]. Subsequent human studies further supported the relevance of ACF by showing that some lesions harbor early APC or KRAS pathway alterations and may precede adenoma formation ref [6], ref [7], ref [8].

An especially informative figure-driven genetic model is the K-rasG12D mouse study of Calcagno et al., in which spontaneous or epithelial-targeted oncogenic K-ras expression generated ACF-like lesions morphologically comparable to azoxymethane (AOM)-induced lesions ref [17]. The visual strength of this model lies in side-by-side comparison of whole-mount and histologic images demonstrating that Kras activation alone can initiate early abnormal crypt architecture, while additional AOM exposure promotes enlargement and dysplastic microadenoma formation preferentially in the proximal colon ref [17]. These figures also highlight a key biological insight often obscured in summary tables: lesion fate is region dependent, with proximal lesions showing greater proliferative signaling and neoplastic potential than distal counterparts ref [17], ref [9], ref [10].

More broadly, such image-based models have clarified that early colorectal carcinogenesis is not represented by a single uniform precursor, but by morphologically similar lesions with distinct molecular trajectories. Integrating lesion photographs, histology, BrdU/TUNEL staining, and pathway readouts such as ERK activation has therefore become a powerful framework for distinguishing innocuous hyperplastic change from progression-prone ACF ref [17], ref [11], ref [12], ref [13]. In survey figures, these multimodal presentations are particularly useful for illustrating how genotype, carcinogen exposure, and colonic subsite jointly shape the earliest steps of colorectal tumor initiation ref [17], ref [14].

Tabulated summaries of dietary carcinogens in colorectal cancer research typically organize evidence by chemical class, food source, target lesion, and experimental endpoint. Among these agents, heterocyclic amines generated during high-temperature cooking of meat are especially important because they connect human dietary exposure to reproducible rodent colon tumor models. PhIP is notable in this context as one of the most abundant mutagenic heterocyclic amines detected in cooked meat and fish and as a compound with direct relevance to colon carcinogenesis tables that compare organotropism across food-borne mutagens ref [1], ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

A key tabulated finding is that chronic dietary administration of PhIP induced colon adenocarcinomas in F344 rats, with particularly high incidence in males, while also producing mammary tumors in females ref [1]. This observation is strengthened by mechanistic entries commonly included in evidence tables: PhIP forms DNA adducts in the colon ref [5], is metabolically activated to genotoxic intermediates by cytochrome P450-dependent pathways ref [6], ref [7], and shows tissue distribution favoring substantial intestinal exposure, including recovery in bile and feces ref [8]. Such data help explain why PhIP has become a benchmark dietary carcinogen in experimental colorectal cancer modeling.

Tables also benefit from recording intermediate lesions and exposure interactions rather than tumor incidence alone. In this regard, PhIP induces aberrant crypt foci in rat colon ref [9], and intestinal adenocarcinomas were also reported in analbuminemic rats ref [10], supporting its use across stages of early and overt carcinogenesis. More broadly, compilations of dietary carcinogens should note that combined low-dose heterocyclic amine exposure can enhance carcinogenic responses ref [11], whereas dietary modifiers such as wheat bran or citrus fiber may suppress aromatic amine-induced intestinal tumorigenesis in rats ref [12]. Finally, epidemiologic syntheses linking meat-rich dietary patterns to colorectal cancer risk provide the translational frame for these experimental tables, even though animal doses exceed typical human exposure ref [13], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Study Design, Synthesis, and Scholarly Apparatus
subsections.content:
Experimental disease models of colorectal cancer (CRC) span carcinogen-induced, transplantation, and genetically engineered systems, each capturing different phases of tumor initiation, progression, and host interaction. Classic chemically induced models, especially azoxymethane (AOM) and the AOM/dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) combination, remain central for studying adenoma–carcinoma evolution and inflammation-associated colorectal tumorigenesis, whereas orthotopic and syngeneic implantation models are preferred for rapid studies of invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic response [ref 1, ref 2, ref 3, ref 4]. Genetically engineered mice centered on Apc loss, alone or combined with Kras, Tp53, or Tgfbr pathway alterations, more closely recapitulate defined molecular subtypes and have been indispensable for mechanism-oriented intervention studies [ref 5, ref 6, ref 7].

Intervention models are increasingly designed to incorporate clinically relevant modifiers beyond primary tumor burden. In CRC, the C26 colon adenocarcinoma model is widely used to study cancer cachexia, systemic inflammation, and treatment tolerance, thereby extending model utility from tumor biology to whole-body therapeutic assessment [ref 8, ref 9]. Notably, Zhang et al. established a compound mouse model combining C26-induced cachexia with traditional Chinese medicine-defined spleen deficiency syndrome, producing aggravated weight loss, muscle atrophy, fat lipolysis, and immune-organ atrophy; this framework also enabled evaluation of atractylenolide I as an anticachectic intervention without major effects on tumor growth [ref 10]. Such composite designs are methodologically important because they better reflect the multimorbidity and host-state heterogeneity often accompanying advanced CRC.

No single model is sufficient for all intervention questions. Xenografts are efficient for drug screening but poorly preserve immune context; syngeneic and orthotopic models restore host immunity and tissue geography; carcinogen-driven and engineered models better represent stepwise pathogenesis and chemoprevention; and composite models incorporating cachexia, microbiota disruption, diet, or syndrome-based host factors can reveal treatment effects that would be obscured in tumor-centric systems alone [ref 3, ref 4, ref 7, ref 9, ref 10]. Accordingly, rigorous study design increasingly relies on matching the intervention endpoint—tumor regression, prevention, metastasis control, toxicity mitigation, or systemic symptom relief—to the biological strengths and limitations of the selected CRC model.

subsections.section_title: Study Design, Synthesis, and Scholarly Apparatus
subsections.content:
Microphysiological systems and organ-on-chip platforms occupy an intermediate position between static 3D culture and whole-animal models by integrating epithelial, stromal, endothelial, and mechanical cues within perfused microfluidic devices. For colorectal cancer (CRC), their main value lies in reconstructing tissue–tissue interfaces, fluid shear, and spatiotemporal gradients that are difficult to reproduce in spheroids or conventional organoids, while remaining more experimentally tractable than in vivo metastasis models [1, 2].

A representative CRC application is the multi-site metastasis-on-a-chip system reported by Aleman and Skardal, in which an on-chip primary CRC construct is connected under recirculating flow to downstream liver, lung, endothelial, and matrix control compartments [1]. In this configuration, HCT116 cells proliferated at the primary site, entered circulation, and preferentially engrafted in liver and lung constructs, reproducing clinically relevant organ tropism while also enabling direct visualization of dissemination and colonization dynamics [1]. Such designs are particularly useful for dissecting the relative contributions of vascular geometry, target-organ microenvironment, and seed-and-soil interactions in CRC metastatic spread [1].

Although the second highlighted study concerns normal intestine rather than CRC per se, it is methodologically important for the field because it shows how biopsy-derived organoids can be matured into a vascularized, perfused intestine-on-chip with polarized epithelium, villus-like architecture, barrier function, mucus secretion, digestive activity, and transcriptomic similarity to native human duodenum that exceeds that of the source organoids alone [2]. For CRC modeling, this illustrates a key design principle: combining patient-derived epithelial material with endothelial co-culture, luminal access, and mechanical stimulation can yield a more physiologically faithful host tissue context for studying tumor initiation, invasion, drug absorption, and toxicity [2].

Current CRC chip platforms remain reductionist, often lacking immune compartments, fibroblast diversity, microbiota, and fully tissue-specific extracellular matrices; moreover, metastatic models still incompletely capture intravasation and extravasation steps [1, 2]. Even so, these systems are increasingly attractive for mechanism-oriented studies and for personalized workflows that link patient-derived organoids to dynamic readouts of invasion, colonization preference, barrier injury, and treatment response. As fabrication, co-culture complexity, and analytical integration improve, organ-on-chip models are likely to become an important complement to organoids and animal models in the experimental repertoire for CRC research [1, 2].

Studies describing colorectal cancer models increasingly report not only species and platform type, but also molecular subtype, anatomical location, and degree of concordance with human disease. For conventional in vitro systems, comparative profiling has shown that colon cancer cell lines can preserve major epigenetic features of primary tumors, including promoter methylation patterns in hMLH1, MGMT, p16INK4a, p14ARF, APC, and CDH1, supporting their continued use as tractable models when subtype context is specified ref [21]. Earlier large-scale characterization of colorectal cancer cell lines likewise emphasized the need to annotate MSI/MSS status and key driver alterations when selecting models for mechanistic or therapeutic studies.

A critical study characteristic is whether the model represents early initiation, progression, or advanced disease. In genetically engineered mouse models, oncogenic K-ras activation in colonic epithelium produces aberrant crypt foci and reveals marked regional heterogeneity: lesions in the proximal colon show enhanced PKCβII expression, MEK/ERK activation, proliferation, and progression potential, whereas distal lesions are more apoptotic and less progression-prone ref [17]. This illustrates how model readouts depend strongly on colonic subsite, a variable that mirrors biological differences between right- and left-sided human colorectal cancers.

Accordingly, robust reporting of model characteristics should include host species or tissue source, derivation strategy, genotype, MSI/CIN/CIMP-related features, tumor location, lesion stage, and whether the system captures stromal, immune, or microbiota components. For cell lines, authentication and molecular annotation are indispensable; for murine models, inducible versus constitutive driver activation and carcinogen exposure should be stated explicitly. Such descriptors determine what questions a model can answer and improve comparability across studies, especially when linking early carcinogenesis models to later-stage translational platforms ref [21], ref [17].

Therapeutic context is a major determinant of how colorectal cancer (CRC) models are interpreted. Experimental systems are commonly deployed not only to test cytotoxic efficacy but also to capture adaptive responses to standard agents such as irinotecan, oxaliplatin, and 5-fluorouracil, as well as targeted drugs directed at EGFR, BRAF, VEGF, or PI3K/AKT signaling. In this setting, the choice of model influences whether investigators observe transient growth arrest, apoptosis, senescence, clonal outgrowth, or microenvironment-driven resistance, all of which are clinically relevant endpoints in advanced CRC [1].

A particularly instructive example is the irinotecan context, where Vétillard et al. showed in CRC cell lines and xenografts that AKT becomes activated during early chemotherapy-induced senescence, and that pharmacologic AKT inhibition enhances irinotecan efficacy, suppresses persistent clone emergence, and shifts cell fate from senescence toward apoptosis through p21 downregulation, NOXA induction, and MCL1 inactivation [1]. These findings complement earlier work indicating that irinotecan can generate more aggressive persistent populations dependent on anti-apoptotic signaling, and that senescence versus apoptosis is itself a treatment-relevant experimental variable rather than a neutral phenotypic readout [2-5].

More broadly, therapeutic studies increasingly require models that match the biological question: conventional 2D lines remain useful for pathway dissection and drug-combination screening; spheroids and organoids better capture drug penetration gradients and patient-specific response heterogeneity; and xenografts or microphysiological systems are needed when stromal, metastatic, or pharmacokinetic influences are central [6-13]. Thus, when summarizing CRC experimental models, the therapeutic and experimental context should record the treatment class, schedule, combination logic, resistance phenotype interrogated, and whether the model is intended for mechanistic discovery, translational prediction, or preclinical validation [1,6,10-13].
